title: Format, length and the "aha" moment
summary: How R1-Zero's simple think-then-answer template and format reward worked, why its answers grew longer and produced an "aha moment", and how the 2025 Dr. GRPO paper showed that part of that growth came from a bias in GRPO's averaging.
learningObjectives: Describe R1-Zero's <think>/<answer> template and its two rule-based rewards, accuracy and format.
Explain why DeepSeek avoided a neural reward model for R1-Zero.
Describe what DeepSeek reported about accuracy, response length and the aha moment during R1-Zero training.
Explain in plain words how dividing each answer's loss by its own length favors short correct answers and long wrong ones.
Choose TRL's loss_type and scale_rewards settings to avoid the length and difficulty biases.
Read length and accuracy curves together and tell real reasoning gains from length drift.

studyGuide.mentalModel: Picture an exam paper with two printed boxes: a big "working" box and a small "final answer" box. The examiner marks only the small box and checks you used both. Over many exams the student learns to fill the working box more and more, because careful working gets more answers right. But there's a quirk in how the marks are spread: a wrong answer's penalty is shared across every line of working, so a student who writes a lot when unsure loses less per line. Some of the extra writing is real care; some is just that quirk. Dr. GRPO fixes the quirk by giving every line the same weight.
keyIdeas: R1-Zero's template only said where to think (<think>) and where to answer (<answer>), not how to think.
Two rule-based rewards: accuracy (is the final answer right?) and format (are the tags used?). A neural reward model was avoided because the policy can learn to fool it.
DeepSeek reported AIME 2024 pass@1 rising from 15.6% to 71.0% (86.7% with majority voting) as thinking grew from hundreds to thousands of tokens.
The aha moment was an intermediate checkpoint that flagged its own mistake and re-checked its approach, with no example of checking ever shown.
Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) found that base models already show aha-style reflection, so RL amplified it rather than inventing it.
Original GRPO divides each answer's loss by its own length, which favors short correct answers and lets long wrong answers off lightly; this artificially grows length, especially for wrong answers.
Dividing advantages by the group standard deviation over-weights questions that are nearly all right or all wrong.
In TRL, loss_type="dr_grpo" (or the default "dapo") removes the per-answer length average, and scale_rewards="none" removes the std division.
misconceptions: "Longer answers mean the model is smarter." Length is a cost; it only helps if accuracy rises with it.
"The format reward teaches the model to reason." It only teaches it to use the boxes; the accuracy reward drives the reasoning.
"The aha moment proves reasoning emerged from nothing." Base models already show this behavior; RL made it more common.
"The length bias makes every answer longer." It mainly lengthens wrong answers and favors short correct ones.
recallPrompts: What were the two rewards used for R1-Zero, and how was each checked?
Why did DeepSeek avoid a neural reward model?
What happened to response length and to AIME accuracy as R1-Zero trained?
In your own words, why does dividing by each answer's length favor long wrong answers?
Which two TRL GRPOConfig options control the biases Dr. GRPO describes?
studyGuide.explainBackPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never trained a model why R1-Zero's answers got longer during training, and why at least part of that growth was not the model "thinking harder". Use the exam-paper picture or your own analogy, and no formulas.

quiz.prompt: What did R1-Zero's training template tell the model?
options: Several worked examples of good step-by-step reasoning to copy
To put its reasoning inside <think> tags and its final answer inside <answer> tags
To keep every answer under 100 tokens
To say "wait" whenever it was unsure
quiz.explanation: The template was deliberately minimal: it said where the thinking and the answer go, not how to think. No examples of reasoning were shown, which is why the behavior that appeared was interesting.

quiz.prompt: Why did DeepSeek use rule-based rewards instead of a neural reward model for R1-Zero?
options: Neural reward models cannot read maths
Rule-based rewards make answers shorter
At large scale the policy can learn to fool a neural reward model (reward hacking), and it adds cost and complexity
TRL does not support neural reward models
quiz.explanation: The paper says a neural reward model may suffer from reward hacking in large-scale RL, and retraining one adds resources and complexity. Code that checks answers is much harder to fool.

quiz.prompt: Under original GRPO averaging, each answer's loss is divided by its own length. Which answer gets the gentlest push per token?
options: A short correct answer
A long correct answer
A short wrong answer
A long wrong answer, among the wrong ones: its penalty is spread over many tokens
quiz.explanation: Spreading a negative advantage across many tokens makes each token's penalty small, so long wrong answers are punished lightly. Over time the model learns to ramble when unsure. (Among correct answers, long ones also get a smaller per-token push, which is why short correct answers are favored.)

quiz.prompt: What did the Dr. GRPO paper report about the "aha moment"?
options: Base models such as DeepSeek-V3-Base already show aha-style self-reflection before RL
It never happened; the quote was invented
It only appears in models larger than 600B parameters
It is caused by the format reward
quiz.explanation: Liu et al. (2025) found aha-style reflection already in base models. RL made the behavior more common rather than creating it from nothing.

quiz.prompt: You want a Dr. GRPO-style run in TRL. Which settings match it?
options: loss_type="grpo" and scale_rewards="group"
beta=0.5 and temperature=0.1
max_completion_length=4096 and num_generations=2
loss_type="dr_grpo" and scale_rewards="none"
quiz.explanation: "dr_grpo" divides token losses by a constant instead of each answer's length, and scale_rewards="none" stops dividing advantages by the group's standard deviation. Those are the two fixes Dr. GRPO proposes.

quiz.prompt: During a run, mean completion length doubles but accuracy stays flat. What's the most sensible reading?
options: Great news: the model has had its aha moment
A warning sign: check whether wrong answers are growing, read some replies, and consider your loss_type
The learning rate is definitely too low
The format reward is broken
quiz.explanation: Length that grows without accuracy is a cost with no benefit. Look at the length of wrong answers separately, read replies for filler, and check the loss averaging.

exercises.title: Close the loopholes in the format reward
hints: Test the lesson's regex on a reply with two <answer> blocks first.
Inside each block, allow any character as long as no tag starts there: (?:(?!</?think>|</?answer>).)*
Use named groups so you can check the thinking length and the answer separately.

exercises.title: Feel the length bias with a calculator
hints: The group mean reward is the average of the four rewards.
Original GRPO: divide the advantage by that answer's own length.
Dr. GRPO: divide every advantage by the same constant, 200.
